title: Class 5 Maths Area and Its Boundary Explained (Same Area, Different Perimeter) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Area and Its Boundary Explained + Quiz
meta_desc: Class 5 Maths Area and Its Boundary made simple: how area differs from perimeter, why shapes share area yet differ in boundary, with a free quiz.
excerpt: Area is the surface a shape covers; its boundary is the edge that runs around it. This NCERT Class 5 chapter turns on one surprising idea — two shapes can share an area yet have very different boundaries. Here is the whole thing, with worked case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Picture two tablecloths on a shop counter. One is a long thin runner, the other a fat square, and both are cut from the very same amount of cloth. Ask a ten-year-old which one needs more lace stitched around its edge and you have walked straight into the heart of NCERT Class 5 Maths Area and Its Boundary. The chapter is not really about formulas. It is about seeing that the flat surface a shape covers and the edge that runs around it are two separate things — and that one can change while the other stays exactly the same.

I have taught this chapter to a lot of Class 5 children, and the same confusion turns up every year: they treat area and boundary as one measurement wearing two names. Once that knot is untied, the rest of the chapter falls into place quickly.

Area is the inside, boundary is the edge

Start with plain language before any numbers. The area of a shape is how much flat surface it covers — the amount of cloth in the tablecloth, the floor a carpet hides, the grass inside a field. We count it in square units: square centimetres, square metres. The boundary is the line that goes all the way around the edge — the lace on the tablecloth, the fence around the field. That is the perimeter, and we measure it in ordinary length units: centimetres, metres.

Two different questions, two different units

The quickest way to keep them apart is to notice they answer different questions and carry different units.

 AreaBoundary (perimeter)
What it measuresThe surface insideThe edge around
Everyday exampleTiles to cover a floorSkirting along the wall
UnitSquare units (sq cm, sq m)Length units (cm, m)
How you find itCount the squares insideAdd up all the side lengths

The big idea: same area, different boundary

Here is the insight the whole chapter is built on, and it genuinely surprises children. Take 12 identical square tiles and arrange them into a rectangle. You can do it three neat ways, and every single one uses all 12 tiles — so the area is always 12 square units. But the boundary is not the same at all.

ArrangementAreaBoundary
1 tile × 12 tiles12 sq units26 units
2 tiles × 6 tiles12 sq units16 units
3 tiles × 4 tiles12 sq units14 units

Same area every time, three different boundaries. The long thin strip has the biggest boundary; the arrangement closest to a square has the smallest. This is exactly why the square tablecloth needs less lace than the thin runner made from the same cloth. It is worth letting a child cut the shapes out and trace the edges — the idea lands far harder when their finger runs the long way around the 1 × 12 strip.

And the reverse: same boundary, different area

The trick works the other way too, which is the part that really cements understanding. Suppose you have a piece of string 16 units long and you bend it into different rectangles. The boundary stays 16 every time, but the space trapped inside changes.

  • A 1 × 7 rectangle: boundary 16, area only 7 sq units.
  • A 2 × 6 rectangle: boundary 16, area 12 sq units.
  • A 4 × 4 square: boundary 16, area a full 16 sq units.

So a long thin shape wastes space; the square-shaped one holds the most. Farmers know this in their bones — given a fixed length of fencing, a squarish field encloses more land than a narrow strip.

Case study: Rani’s kitchen tiles

Now let us use it the way the case-study questions do. Rani is tiling her kitchen floor, which is 4 metres long and 3 metres wide, using square tiles of side 1 metre. She also wants to run a wooden skirting strip along the bottom of all four walls.

How many tiles does she need? The floor is a rectangle, so the area is 4 × 3 = 12 square metres. Each tile covers 1 square metre, so she needs 12 tiles.

How much skirting? The skirting runs along the boundary, so we add the four sides: 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 metres. Notice the two answers use different units — 12 square metres of tile, 14 metres of skirting. Mixing those units up is the single most common mistake I see, so I always make children say the unit out loud.

Case study: choosing the field to fence

A farmer near Nashik has two plots, each with an area of 36 square metres. One plot is a 6 m × 6 m square; the other is a long 12 m × 3 m strip. Fencing costs the same per metre for both. Which plot is cheaper to fence?

Both hold the same 36 square metres of crop, so area does not decide it. The boundary does. The square plot has a perimeter of 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 metres. The long strip has a perimeter of 12 + 3 + 12 + 3 = 30 metres. The square is cheaper to fence by 6 metres of material, even though it grows exactly as much. That is the same-area-different-boundary idea earning its keep in real life.

A quick way to avoid the classic slip

Before writing any answer, get your child to ask one question: am I covering the inside or walking around the edge? Covering means area, and the unit must be square. Walking the edge means boundary, and the unit is plain length. That one habit fixes more marks in this chapter than any amount of formula drilling.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly these ideas — telling area from boundary, spotting same-area-different-perimeter, and reading a simple word problem. Let your child attempt it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer practice, the printable case-study e-book at the end walks through many more real-life situations, each with a full worked solution.

quiz.title: Class 5 Area and Its Boundary Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on telling area from boundary and the same-area, different-perimeter idea. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 5 Maths — Area and Its Boundary

questions.q: A rectangle is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a rectangle is length times width: 5 × 3 = 15 square centimetres.

questions.q: What is the boundary (perimeter) of the same 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle?
questions.explanation: Add all four sides: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. Boundary is measured in plain length units.

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure area?
questions.explanation: Area is a surface, so it is counted in square units such as the square metre.

questions.q: Two shapes cover the same area. Must they have the same boundary?
options: No, the boundary can be different
questions.explanation: Same area does not mean same boundary. A 3 by 4 and a 1 by 12 rectangle both cover 12 sq units but have different perimeters.

questions.q: A square field has a side of 6 m. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: A square has four equal sides: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 m.

questions.q: What is the area of that same square field with side 6 m?
questions.explanation: Area of a square is side times side: 6 × 6 = 36 square metres.

questions.q: Rani has 12 square tiles. Which arrangement needs the least edging (smallest boundary)?
questions.explanation: The arrangement closest to a square has the smallest boundary. The 3 by 4 rectangle has a perimeter of 14, less than the long strips.

questions.q: A vegetable field is 8 m long and 2 m wide. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area is length times width: 8 × 2 = 16 square metres.

faq.q: What is the difference between area and boundary in Class 5 Maths?
faq.a: Area is the flat surface a shape covers, counted in square units like square metres. The boundary is the edge running all the way around the shape, measured in plain length units like metres. They answer different questions, so they carry different units.

faq.q: Can two shapes have the same area but different perimeter?
faq.a: Yes, and this is the main idea of the chapter. A 3 m × 4 m rectangle and a 1 m × 12 m rectangle both cover 12 square metres, but their boundaries are 14 m and 26 m. The shape closest to a square always has the smallest boundary.

faq.q: How do you find the area of a rectangle?
faq.a: Multiply the length by the width. For a floor 4 m by 3 m, the area is 4 × 3 = 12 square metres. If the shape is drawn on squared paper, you can instead count how many unit squares fit inside it.

faq.q: Which chapter of NCERT Class 5 Maths is Area and Its Boundary?
faq.a: It is Chapter 11 in the NCERT Class 5 Maths textbook, Math-Magic. It builds on earlier ideas about shapes and length, and it prepares children for perimeter and area work in Class 6 and beyond.
